title: Multispeaker annotation guidelines (draft)
content:
Context: personal draft for how we label messy, multi-party chat transcripts. Mostly for small-adjudicator team and quick sanity checks; NOT final. Keep informal notes + examples to iterate with Ethan/Sofia.

Goals:
- Define consistent rules for speaker attribution, overlapping speech, system messages, and micro-utterances (laughs, emojis, filler tokens).
- Capture provenance when an utterance originates from an export transformation (ASR, webhook, merged threads).
- Quick heuristics for when to split vs. merge turns and when to assign 'ambiguous' label.

High-level rules (proposal):
1) Speaker tokenization
   - If speaker metadata is explicit (speaker_id or name), respect it. Use provided name unless clearly wrong.
   - If speaker is missing: infer from turn boundaries and punctuation. If uncertain, tag speaker as "SPEAKER_UNKNOWN" and add note.
   - When two participants appear in one line separated by colons ("A: ... B: ..."), split into two turns.

2) Overlapping speech / interruptions
   - Mark interruptions as new turn if there is an explicit marker ([interrupt], dash, ellipsis) or if the ASR provides overlapping timestamps.
   - For short overlap (< 1s) where semantics continue, merge into the preceding or following turn depending on where the primary clause resolves. Record provenance.

3) System / meta messages (e.g., "bot joined", "message edited")
   - Label these as METADATA and do not use them for intent classification.
   - If a system message contains user-visible content ("bot: here's the link"), split into METADATA + USER_CONTENT where appropriate.

4) Partial utterances and non-sentences
   - Short fillers ("uh", "mm", "hmm") tag as FILLER. Do not treat as main content unless the downstream task expects prosody.
   - Punctuation-only messages ("...", "!!!") -> tag as EMOTIVE. Add "emphasis":true metadata (we capture emphasis as a label line in our system).

5) Emojis, laughter, and paralinguistic tokens
   - Treat emojis as tokens with normalized codepoints (e.g., ":smile:"). If emoji changes intent, annotate with a secondary tag EMOJI_DISAMBIG.
   - Laughter tokens ("haha", "lol", "<laugh>") -> LAUGH tag; when paired with content, keep as separate token appended to content with a spacer.

6) Code switches and fragments in other languages
   - Mark span language if it is >2 words in a different language; otherwise mark as inline code-switch token.

Labeling examples (quick):
- Example 1 (clear multi-turn):
  "A: hey can you send the report? B: on it, give me 10m"
  -> turn1 speaker:A content:"hey can you send the report?"
  -> turn2 speaker:B content:"on it, give me 10m"

- Example 2 (system message + user):
  "bot: meeting created by Alex at 3pm"
  -> METADATA: "meeting created by Alex at 3pm" (if not user-authored)
  -> If Alex posted it herself: USER Alex: "meeting created..." (use provenance)

- Example 3 (interruption):
  "U1: I think we should—
   U2: Wait, not that."
  -> U1: content truncated, label PARTIAL + PROV:ASR_TIMESTAMP
  -> U2: content "Wait, not that." (separate turn)

- Example 4 (emoji changes meaning):
  "Sure, thanks 🙂" -> content: "Sure, thanks" + EMOJI: ":slightly_smiling_face:" + tag: POLITENESS_AFFIRM

Ambiguity heuristics (when to mark AMBIGUOUS):
- No speaker metadata and the text looks like a reply but lacks quoting markers.
- Merged exports where multiple channels appended and we cannot align timestamps.
- Non-linguistic noise that appears as tokens ("[noise]", "<inaudible>") with length > 3 tokens and no context.

Provenance capture (cheap):
- Always add a provenance string on labels: one of [ORIG_UI, ASR, WEBHOOK, MERGE_TOOL] as a flat token in the annotation.
- Example: label_provenance:ASR|confidence:0.72 (we store confidence in separate numeric column downstream; here just note provenance string if available).

Quality checks / adjudicator quicklist:
- If a turn contains personal info (PII) and was transformed (redacted/hashed), confirm original source tag and leave a comment: "PII_REDACTED_FROM_ASR".
- When splitting turns, check that punctuation and clause boundaries are preserved; if a split creates a sentence fragment that loses meaning, keep merged and add NOTE: split_harmful=true.

Open questions (needs conversation with product & SRE):
- How to represent simultaneous messages with identical timestamps? Currently plan: preserve both as separate turns but mark as SIMUL_SAME_TS. Need to ensure dedupe logic in downstream evals.
- Standardize provenance codes across exports. Should we use full URIs or short codes? Short codes preferred for CSVs but painful for audit.
- Does downstream NLU want filler tokens removed or preserved? We should create a toggled pipeline: RAW vs. CLEANED.

Edge-case sample bank (for test set):
- Transcript where a single message contains multiple labelled sub-sentences belonging to different intents ("Book flight tomorrow and btw what's the wifi password?") -> annotate as two intents with same speaker and mark primary intent by priority.
- ASR mis-segmentation: long run-on turned into one huge line -> create synthetic splits using punctuation heuristics and then flag for human review.
- Thread merge: messages from two channels pasted together with no separator -> label as MERGED_EXPORT and sample for adjudication.

Implementation notes for label UI (quick):
- Show provenance badge next to each turn.
- Provide quick buttons: SPLIT TURN, MERGE WITH PREV, MARK AMBIGUOUS, FLAG METADATA.
- When adjudicator presses SPLIT: require them to add a short rationale (2–6 words) for auditability.

Next steps / Todo (me/Ethan/Sofia):
- Ethan: prototype PROV badge in the labeling UI (JIRA-ANNO-342).
- Sofia: export 200 real, messy transcripts for edge-case bank (deadline: 2026-03-10).
- Me (Ava): consolidate adjudicator notes into a short checklist + training slide (1 page) and sync with product.

Notes to self: keep this doc lean. Convert to Confluence draft once heuristics settle; prefer to keep concrete examples there. For now, add new weird cases as separate bullet items rather than rewriting sections.

End of draft.
